events.text: Before the ancestral tablets, with the whole house kneeling behind, you name {npc} Heir Apparent. The incense smoke bends toward {him} as if the old names on the tablets lean down to look. {npc} does not move for a long moment, and then bows until {his} forehead touches the cold floor.

choices.text: Lift {him} up with your own hands

mem.note: lifted me up before the tablets

effects.log: {npc} rises. For the first time {he} looks at you as one who will one day stand where you stand.

choices.text: Let {him} stay down until the incense burns out

mem.note: taught me the weight of the seat

effects.log: The incense burns a long time. When {npc} rises, {his} knees are stiff and {his} eyes are very clear.

choices.text: Tell {him} the seat is a burden, not a prize

mem.note: told me the truth about the seat

effects.log: "I know," {npc} says, which is what everyone says, and nobody knows until later.

events.text: You hand {npc} the keys of the treasury: an iron ring of them, some older than the house itself, one that opens nothing anyone can remember. As Steward of the Treasury {he} will keep the fields, the shops and every coin. {npc} weighs the ring in one hand and says, "Show me the books."

effects.log: You sit up half the night over the ledgers. By dawn {npc} has found two errors and a cousin who owes you rent.
"Every steward is tempted," you say. "The good ones are bored by it." {npc} laughs, a little too quickly.
You leave {npc} with the ring and the books. The lamp in the counting room burns until the small hours.

events.text: The courtyard is swept, the practice swords laid out in a row. You name {npc} Master of Arms, and the clan's young ones line up in front of {him}, the smallest at the end, holding a stick because no sword fits yet.

mem.note: crossed swords with me before the children

effects.log: You cross blunted swords with {npc} while the children hold their breath. You let nobody win. They will talk of it for years.

choices.text: Hand the smallest one a real sword

mem.note: trusted me with the smallest one

effects.log: {npc} looks at you, then kneels to show the little one how to hold it. That is the first lesson of the Master of Arms.

choices.text: Tell {him} to be hard on them

effects.log: "Hard is easy," {npc} says. "I will be fair." You find you like that answer better.

events.text: The ancestral hall is cold and smells of old incense. You name {npc} Keeper of the Ancestral Hall: the tablets, the rites, the register of the dead and the names nobody says aloud. {npc} runs a fingertip along the oldest tablet and finds no dust on it. "Someone has been doing this already," {he} says.

mem.note: kept the tablets myself, in secret

effects.log: For years you have dusted the tablets yourself at night. {npc} looks at you differently afterwards.

choices.text: Tell {him} to keep the hall better than you did

effects.log: {npc} bows. The next morning the hall smells of fresh incense and new paper.

choices.text: Read the oldest names aloud together

mem.note: read the old names aloud with me

effects.log: You read the names until your voices are hoarse. Some of them you had never heard. Now they are said again.

events.text: A new travelling coat, a seal of the clan on a cord, a list of the houses that matter and the ones that only think they do. You name {npc} Envoy. "Carry our name well," you say. {npc} turns the seal over. "And if they spit on it?"

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly. "Clean," {he} repeats, as if tasting the word.
{npc} smiles. It is not a kind smile. The house has an envoy with a long memory.
You spend a week on bows and forms of address. By the end {npc} can insult anyone so politely that they thank {him}.

events.text: After the naming of the Heir Apparent, {npc} stays behind in the ancestral hall when everyone else has gone. You find {him} there at midnight, sitting in front of the tablets with {his} back very straight. "I am older," {he} says without turning. "I have always been older."

effects.log: You sit together until the candles gutter. Nothing is settled. Something is softer.

choices.text: Explain why you chose as you did

effects.log: You give your reasons. {npc} listens to every one of them, nods, and does not believe a word.
"Yes," {npc} says. "I heard." {He} gets up and leaves, and does not bow.

events.text: {npc} is at the gate the morning after the naming, saddlebags packed, as if for a long journey. "Just visiting a friend," {he} says. Nobody in the house has heard of the friend. Everyone knows which office {he} did not get.

choices.text: Ask {him} to stay for the evening meal

effects.log: {npc} hesitates, then unpacks one bag. Only one.

choices.text: Offer {him} the next office that falls vacant

effects.log: {npc} weighs it. "The next one," {he} says. "I will hold you to it."
{npc} rides out without looking back. The friend, it turns out, lives very close to a house that hates yours.

events.text: At the evening meal {npc} raises a cup to the new office-holder and says all the right words in exactly the wrong voice. Two of the servants drop a dish. Your own children look at their bowls. Every family has a night like this.

choices.text: Drink the toast as if it were sincere

effects.log: You drink. {npc} drinks. Everyone breathes again, more or less.
In the corridor {npc} says, "You never once asked me what I wanted." You realise it is true.
The house goes very quiet. {npc} apologises, perfectly, and you know you have made it worse.

events.text: {npc} lays the year's books in front of you with the air of someone setting down a sword after a long fight. The fields paid, the shops paid, a debt from three generations back has been collected with interest and a written apology. "The treasury," {he} says, "is fat."

choices.text: Praise {him} in front of the house

effects.log: {npc} goes red to the ears and spends the rest of the evening pretending not to be pleased.

choices.text: Ask how the old debt was collected

effects.log: "Politely," {npc} says, "and twice." You decide not to ask the second part.

choices.text: Put part of it aside for the children

effects.log: You set aside a chest for the young ones' schooling. {npc} writes it in the books in red ink: untouchable.

events.text: The books do not add up. You find the missing silver in a place no Steward should keep it: a new roof on a house {npc} bought quietly in the next town, under another name. When you ask, {npc} looks at the floor for a long time.

effects.log: {npc} pays back what {he} can, and signs a paper for the rest. {His} hand shakes.
"Because it was there," {npc} says finally, "and because nobody ever looked." You start looking.
{npc} weeps, which you did not expect, and swears on the ancestral tablets. Whether {he} keeps it is another matter.

events.text: At the year's end the Master of Arms holds a little contest in the courtyard. The clan's young ones fight each other with blunted swords while {npc} walks between them, correcting a foot here, an elbow there. Even the smallest one lands a clean blow.

choices.text: Give the winners a sweet each

effects.log: Everyone wins, in the end. {npc} pretends to disapprove and eats one too.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to show you something new

effects.log: {npc} shows you a feint {he} invented over the winter. It is good. You tell {him} so.
You lose, on purpose, very convincingly. The winner will remember it all their life.

events.text: One of the clan's young ones comes home from practice with a split lip and won't say who did it. You find out anyway: the Master of Arms, {npc}, drilled them until they dropped, and then drilled them again. "The world will not go easy on them," {npc} says. "Why should I?"

choices.text: Tell {him} there is hard and there is cruel

effects.log: {npc} listens with {his} jaw set. The next day the drills are shorter. Not much shorter.

choices.text: Back {him} in front of the children

effects.log: The children stop complaining. They also stop laughing in the courtyard.

choices.text: Take over the drills for a week yourself

effects.log: You teach for a week. {npc} watches from the gallery, arms folded, and learns something.

events.text: On the night of the year's last rite {npc} reads the register of the dead aloud in the ancestral hall, every name, with the year of each death and one thing each person was known for. When {he} reaches the names of people you knew, {his} voice does not change. Somehow that is what undoes you.

choices.text: Add a name {he} did not know

effects.log: You tell {npc} of someone the register forgot. {He} writes it in, carefully, with a fresh brush.

choices.text: Stay in the hall after the rite

effects.log: You sit with the tablets until dawn. Something in you that has been tight for years lets go a little.
{npc} only nods. Keepers of halls do not expect thanks. That is why it matters.

events.text: The rites have lapsed. The incense in the ancestral hall is a month old, a tablet has cracked and nobody noticed, and {npc} was seen at a teahouse on the day of the spring offering. The elders of the house are talking, and they are talking to you.

choices.text: Do the rites yourself, in front of {him}

effects.log: You kneel and light the incense without a word. {npc} kneels beside you, scarlet, and does not miss another.
"I sit with the dead all day," {npc} says. "Sometimes I forget the living." You walk {him} to the market the next morning.

choices.text: Have the cracked tablet mended in gold

effects.log: The crack is filled with gold. It is more beautiful than before, which the elders find suspicious.

events.text: {npc} comes home from a long round of visits with a bundle of letters and a story for each one. A house that would not answer your letters for twenty years has sent a gift of tea. Another wants to talk about a marriage. "I did nothing," {npc} says. "I drank their tea and admired their gardens."

effects.log: {npc} bows with great dignity and a grin {he} cannot quite hide.
It is very polite and asks for a great deal. You put it in the box for things to think about.
{npc} groans, packs, and is gone again before the tea is finished.

events.text: {npc} comes home early from a visit, with a torn sleeve and a stiff face. At a feast in another house a cousin of theirs said something about your family, and {npc} said something back, and then there was a table on the floor. "They started it," {npc} says, which is true and helps nobody.

choices.text: Send an apology with a gift

effects.log: The other house accepts the gift and keeps the grudge. Still, the gift helped.
"Then they will finish it," you say. {npc} looks at you as if you had given {him} a sword.

choices.text: Take the seal back for a season

effects.log: {npc} hands it over without a word. The house is quieter. So is {npc}, for a long time.

events.text: You find {npc}, the Heir Apparent, in your study at night, reading your letters by lamplight. Not to spy. To learn. "I wanted to see how you answer the hard ones," {he} says, and holds up a letter you never answered at all.

effects.log: You write the answer together, crossing out half of it. It is the best letter you have ever sent.

choices.text: Tell {him} some letters are answered by silence

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it, and puts the letter back exactly where it was. A good sign.
{npc} goes. In the morning you find {his} notes on your desk, very neat, about how you answer the hard ones.

events.text: The Heir Apparent, {npc}, has started giving orders in your name. Small ones: a servant dismissed, a field leased, a guest turned away at the gate. Each one is the right order. None of them was {his} to give.

effects.log: {npc} bows. "For now," {he} says, very softly, and you are not sure you were meant to hear.

choices.text: Give {him} one matter of {his} own to rule

effects.log: You give {npc} the eastern fields. {He} rules them well and gives no more orders in your name.
You were the same at that age. You do not tell {npc} that. It would only make it worse.

events.text: It is an ordinary year for the office {npc} holds: nothing won, nothing lost, the work done and the work left over. At the year's end {npc} brings you the account of it anyway, written out by hand, as if afraid you might think {he} had not tried.

effects.log: You read it all. Ordinary years hold a house up more than the famous ones. You say so.
{npc} has a list ready. Of course {he} does.
You set it aside. Later never comes. {npc} notices.

events.text: {npc} has been sick half the winter and still dragged {him}self to the work of the office every day, wrapped in three coats. The year was poor for it. The house noticed something else.

effects.log: {npc} argues, loses, and sleeps for two days. When {he} gets up, {he} works better.
You sit by {npc} with the bowl until it is empty. Neither of you mentions the office.
Brothers, sisters and cousins share the work for a season. It is clumsy and slow and very good for them.

events.text: {npc} no longer eats at the same table as the one who got the office {he} wanted. Two tables, now, in the same hall, and the servants carry each dish twice. The children of the house have started choosing sides by where they sit.

choices.text: Have the two tables pushed together

effects.log: You have the tables joined. They eat at opposite ends of the longest table the house has ever seen.
{npc} looks up, startled. It is the first time in a year {he} has smiled at you.
You ignore it. The tables move further apart.

events.text: A servant brings you a letter {npc} wrote to an old friend, and the servant should not have it. It says nothing terrible. It says: the house is run by the wrong people, and one day that will change.

choices.text: Burn it unread by anyone else

effects.log: You burn it, and dismiss the servant for carrying letters that are not theirs. {npc} never learns why.
{npc} goes white, then red. "Read it," {he} says. "I meant it." At least it is said aloud now.
You keep it in a drawer. You do not know what for, which is how these things start.

events.text: In the courtyard, at the morning drill, {npc} and the one {he} resents are paired by accident. They bow. They begin. It is meant to be practice, and for a moment it is not, and the whole house stops to watch.

effects.log: You catch both blades on your sleeve. "Again," you say, "and slower." They obey. The house breathes.
They finish. Nobody is hurt. Nobody is satisfied either.
{npc} goes, stiff-backed. On the road you talk for the first time in a year.

events.text: The house wakes to find {npc}'s rooms empty. A letter on the table, folded once: {he} is not leaving the family, {he} writes, only the house. The family name is still {his}. The gate, for now, is not.

effects.log: You catch {npc} at the river ferry. You do not bring {him} back. You do make {him} promise to write.
You tell the servants not to touch anything. The rooms wait. So do you.
The Keeper asks if {npc}'s name should be struck. "No," you say. "Never."

events.text: It ends the way these things end in old houses: in the ancestral courtyard at dawn, with blunted swords, the elders watching from the gallery, and the whole house pretending not to. {npc} and the one {he} resents bow to the tablets, then to each other. When it is over, it is over.

effects.log: You bind them side by side on the courtyard steps. Neither says sorry. Both stay for the meal.

choices.text: Have the duel written in the register

effects.log: The Keeper writes it in: the day, the names, the end of it. Old houses keep these things.
You say nothing, which in this house says everything.

events.text: You come down to the well at dawn and find {npc} and the one {he} has not spoken to in years sharing a jar of wine and arguing about an uncle who died before either of them was born. Neither of them looks at you. The feud seems to be over. You decide not to ask how.

effects.log: They make room for you on the edge of the well. The uncle, it turns out, was a scoundrel.
You go back to bed and sleep better than you have in years.

events.text: For the first time every office of the house is held by its own blood: the Heir Apparent, the Steward of the Treasury, the Master of Arms, the Keeper of the Ancestral Hall, the Envoy. At the year's feast they sit in a row at the high table, bickering like children, and the old servants weep openly into the soup.

choices.text: Raise a cup to all five

effects.log: You raise a cup. They raise five. Somebody spills theirs. It is perfect.

choices.text: Have a painting made of them

effects.log: A painter is hired. They argue about who stands where for a whole month.
You kneel before the tablets that night and tell the old names that the house is whole.

events.text: You held the keys of the treasury for years before you held the house. You know which field floods, which shop lies about its takings, which cousin will ask for a loan at the new year. The new Steward comes to you with the books, and you find you already know what is in them.

effects.log: You spend a month over the ledgers. The new Steward will be better than you were. That is the point.

choices.text: Keep a set of books of your own

effects.log: You keep a second set, quietly. Old habits. The house is safer for it, and less trusting.

events.text: You were the Master of Arms. The children of the house still call you that, even now you are its head, and they still line up in the courtyard when you walk through it, in case you mean to drill them.

choices.text: Drill them, like in the old days

effects.log: You drill them until they drop and then let them win. The courtyard rings like it used to.

choices.text: Name a new Master of Arms soon

effects.log: You watch the courtyard from the gallery now. It is harder than drilling it.

events.text: You kept the ancestral hall for years. Now your own parent's tablet stands in it, new and pale among the old dark ones, and it is someone else's work to dust it. You do it anyway, every night, the way you always did.

effects.log: You read it aloud in the empty hall. It sounds like any other name on the tablets now. That is the hardest part.

choices.text: Write one more line in the register

effects.log: You write down one thing your parent was known for. You write it small, so it will fit.

events.text: You carried the family's name to every house that mattered. Now you are the name. The first letter that comes to the new head of the house is from a family you once charmed over a garden, offering their condolences, and a marriage.

choices.text: Answer it in your own hand

effects.log: You write back as you always did. They will know the hand. That is the point.
You send someone else to drink their tea. It is strange, being the one who waits for news.

events.text: You were named Heir Apparent years ago, before the tablets, and you have waited for this seat as long as you can remember. Now it is yours. You sit in it for the first time and find it much harder than it looked, and much lonelier.

effects.log: You sit through the night. By dawn it is a chair again, and you are its owner.

choices.text: Call your brothers and sisters in

effects.log: You call them in, one by one, and ask each of them what they want. Your parent never did.

events.text: All your life you were passed over: never the Heir Apparent, never handed a key or a seal. Now the house is yours anyway, by blood and by the turn of things. The ones who held the offices come to you one by one, unsure what you remember.

choices.text: Keep them all in their offices

effects.log: You keep every one of them where they are. "I know what it is to be passed over," you say. They will not forget it.

choices.text: Give the offices to new hands

effects.log: You give the offices to those who were passed over, like you. The old holders bow, and remember.

events.text: You held no office in your parent's house. The offices are still there: a Steward with the keys, a Master of Arms in the courtyard, a Keeper in the cold hall, perhaps an Envoy on the road. They wait to hear what the new head wants of them.

choices.text: Ask each of them what the office needs

effects.log: You listen to each one for an afternoon. It is the first time anyone asked.

choices.text: Let them carry on as before

effects.log: The house goes on as it did. Sometimes that is the kindest order.

events.text: {npc} was named Heir Apparent before the ancestral tablets, years ago. Now the seat is yours, and the name on the office means nothing. {npc} comes to the first gathering of the house in mourning white, kneels, and says the words of loyalty perfectly. Nobody in the hall believes them.

choices.text: Raise {him} up and give {him} a seat beside you

effects.log: {npc} sits beside you. It will not be enough. It is something.

choices.text: Accept the words and nothing more

effects.log: {npc} rises, bows, and goes to sit at the far end of the hall.
"What was promised," {npc} says. At least now you both know.

events.text: A year after you took the seat {npc}, who was once Heir Apparent, still keeps the office's seal in a box by {his} bed. A servant tells you. You do not know whether it is grief or a plan.

effects.log: You let {npc} keep the seal. It is only wood and jade. You hope.
{npc} gives it back without a word. Then {he} asks for a field of {his} own, and you give it.

events.text: A letter comes up through the clouds from the house below, in the Steward's careful hand: the fields paid, the Master of Arms has three new students, the Keeper dusted your tablet as if you were dead, which you are not, probably. The letter is already forty years old by your reckoning. It reads like yesterday.

effects.log: You write back. By the time it arrives, the Steward who wrote to you will be very old, or gone.

choices.text: Keep it with your few treasures

effects.log: You keep it with the very few things you brought up from below.

events.text: Word comes from far below: your house still holds its offices, generation after generation, in the order you set. A great-grandchild you never met is Keeper of the Ancestral Hall now, and keeps a tablet for you, just in case.

effects.log: Just in case. You like the child already.
You send down what blessing an immortal can. Below, the incense burns straight for a year.
